newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss wages seen stagnating in 1997 - UBS survey.
newsitem.headline: Swiss wages seen stagnating in 1997 - UBS survey.

text.p: Swiss nominal wages are expected to approximately stagnate on average in 1997, according to a survey by Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS), the bank's chief economist said.

Speaking to the Swiss-American Chamber of Commerce, Peter Buomberger said the broad-based survey showed the highest wage rises would take place in the insurance, information and mineral oil sectors with an average nominal rise of 1.5 percent.
The bottom of the scale was seen in the textile, construction, hotel and airline sectors, where wages in some cases are likely to decline, a statement from the chamber said.

For the first time wages in the federal and cantonal governments were expected to decline, but the range between the cantons, or regions, is wide and goes from wage rises of two percent to falls of three percent.

Buomberger said wage flexibility was a very important element in solving unemployment problems long-term against a backdrop of economic stagnation, massive structural adjustments and continued high unemployment.
Wage flexibility in Switzerland -- defined as the extent and speed with which wages adjust to changes in productivity and the labour market -- is probably still not high enough, he noted.
A recent OECD study showed wage flexibility in Switzerland was higher than in many other European countries, but still significantly lower than in the United States.

Buomberger called for further measures to increase wage flexibility, such as lower starting wages, wider differences within companies, but also more labour mobility within Switzerland and between Switzerland and its European neighbors.
